title.heading: Why the Romans built Hadrian’s Wall
title.lead: What can a wall keep out?

picture.shows: Hadrian’s Wall today, shown in colour across the countryside near Housesteads
picture.subject: named

slides.heading: A frontier in northern Britain
slides.lead: Emperor Hadrian ordered building to begin in AD 122.
points: Hadrian’s Wall stood in northern Britain, in what is now northern England.
It stretched from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth.

figure.shows: Hadrian’s Wall near Housesteads in the landscape today
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: Where was Hadrian’s Wall?
slides.caption: The wall marked a frontier across northern Roman Britain.

figure.intent: Show a north-up map of Britain with a small north arrow. Shade Roman-controlled land south of Hadrian’s Wall differently from land to its north. Mark Hadrian’s Wall accurately from the River Tyne near modern Wallsend to the Solway Firth near Bowness-on-Solway. Label Britain, River Tyne, Solway Firth and Hadrian’s Wall. Show the modern England–Scotland border as a light dashed reference line, labelled Modern border, clearly north of the wall. Do not suggest the wall stood on that border.
figure.alt: Hadrian’s Wall crosses northern Britain from the River Tyne in the east to the Solway Firth in the west, south of today’s England–Scotland border.

slides.heading: Why did Romans build the wall?

items.head: Defence
items.line: The wall made raids into Roman land more difficult.

items.head: Movement
items.line: Soldiers checked people entering Roman land through gates.

items.head: Trade
items.line: Soldiers could check traders’ goods and collect taxes there.

slides.heading: Forts housed the soldiers
slides.lead: Forts were large army bases along Hadrian’s Wall.
points: Barracks gave soldiers places to live and sleep.
Soldiers left forts to patrol and guard gates.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of a Roman fort beside Hadrian’s Wall, with soldiers leaving its gate
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Small buildings helped soldiers guard the wall

sides.title: Milecastles
sides.text: Gates stood about one Roman mile apart, guarded.

picture.shows: A reconstruction of a milecastle on Hadrian’s Wall, a small enclosed guarded gateway
picture.subject: generic

sides.title: Watchtowers
sides.text: Soldiers watched for danger between the milecastles.

picture.shows: A reconstruction of a watchtower on Hadrian’s Wall with soldiers looking over the countryside
picture.subject: generic

myth.claim: The wall stopped everyone from entering Roman land.
myth.fact: People could pass through guarded gates, where Roman soldiers checked them and their goods.

slides.heading: What was a wall gate meant to let soldiers do?

options.text: Allow people through after checking them and their goods.
Keep every person out, even those coming to trade.
options.why: The pupil treats the frontier as a complete ban on crossing rather than a controlled crossing.

options.text: Allow traders through without checking them or their goods.
options.why: The pupil knows trade could continue but misses the soldiers’ role in checking crossings and goods.

items.question: A trader arrives with wool to sell through a wall gate. How should soldiers handle this arrival, and why?
items.answer: Soldiers should check the trader and the wool to control entry and trade, collecting any tax due.

items.question: Soldiers need somewhere to sleep and somewhere to watch distant countryside. Which buildings suit these jobs, and why?
items.answer: Forts provide barracks for sleeping, while watchtowers let soldiers look out for danger.

items.question: Where in Britain was Hadrian’s Wall, and when did building begin?
How did guarded gates help Romans control trade across their frontier?
items.answer: Soldiers could check traders’ goods and collect taxes at the gates.

items.question: Which building would guard a crossing about every Roman mile?
